Chapter: Ch2 Cell: The Building Block of Life
Definition: Minimum distance between two objects that allows them to be seen as distinct; determines the useful magnification of a microscope

Chapter: Ch2 Cell: The Building Block of Life
Definition: Microscope using visible light and glass lenses; magnifies up to ~1000×; used for routine cell observation

Definition: Microscope using electrons instead of light; much higher resolution; allows observation of fine ultrastructure of the cell

Chapter: Ch2 Cell: The Building Block of Life
Definition: Outermost membrane of animal cells; selectively controls entry and exit of materials; made of lipids and proteins

Chapter: Ch2 Cell: The Building Block of Life
Definition: Property of the plasma membrane allowing some substances to pass through freely while restricting others

Chapter: Ch2 Cell: The Building Block of Life
Definition: Spontaneous movement of a substance from a region of high concentration to a region of low concentration down a concentration gradient

Chapter: Ch2 Cell: The Building Block of Life
Definition: Net diffusion of water molecules across a selectively permeable membrane from a region of higher water concentration to lower water concentration

Chapter: Ch2 Cell: The Building Block of Life
Definition: Difference in concentration of a substance between two regions; drives diffusion and osmosis

Definition: Solution having the same water concentration as the cell; no net movement of water occurs; cell stays same size

Chapter: Ch2 Cell: The Building Block of Life

Chapter: Ch2 Cell: The Building Block of Life
Definition: Model describing the plasma membrane as a phospholipid bilayer with proteins embedded in and on it; membrane is flexible and dynamic

Chapter: Ch2 Cell: The Building Block of Life
Definition: Double layer of phospholipid molecules forming the basic structural framework of the cell membrane

Chapter: Ch2 Cell: The Building Block of Life
Definition: Rigid outer layer present outside the plasma membrane in plant, fungal and bacterial cells; mainly composed of cellulose in plants; provides structural support

Chapter: Ch2 Cell: The Building Block of Life
Definition: Complex polysaccharide that is the main component of plant cell walls; provides strength and rigidity

Chapter: Ch2 Cell: The Building Block of Life
Definition: Fluid content inside the plasma membrane excluding the nucleus; contains cell organelles and dissolved substances

Chapter: Ch2 Cell: The Building Block of Life
Definition: Cell type lacking a membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles; e.g., bacteria; nuclear region called nucleoid

Chapter: Ch2 Cell: The Building Block of Life
Definition: Cell type with a well-defined nucleus surrounded by nuclear membrane and membrane-bound organelles; e.g., plant and animal cells

Definition: Poorly defined nuclear region in prokaryotic cells where only nucleic acids (DNA) are located; lacks nuclear membrane

Chapter: Ch2 Cell: The Building Block of Life
Definition: Membrane-bound organelle in eukaryotes containing chromosomes; controls cell activities and heredity; has nuclear membrane and nucleolus

Chapter: Ch2 Cell: The Building Block of Life
Definition: Double-layered membrane surrounding the nucleus in eukaryotic cells; has pores for transfer of materials between nucleus and cytoplasm

Chapter: Ch2 Cell: The Building Block of Life
Definition: Dense, rounded structure inside the nucleus; involved in ribosome production and RNA synthesis

Chapter: Ch2 Cell: The Building Block of Life
Definition: Rod-shaped structures visible during cell division; contain DNA and proteins; carry genetic information from parent to offspring

Chapter: Ch2 Cell: The Building Block of Life
Definition: Deoxyribonucleic acid; molecule that carries genetic information; functional segments called genes; present as chromatin in non-dividing cells

Chapter: Ch2 Cell: The Building Block of Life
Definition: Functional segments of DNA that contain instructions for making proteins and determining traits

Chapter: Ch2 Cell: The Building Block of Life
Definition: Network of DNA and protein in non-dividing cell nucleus; condenses to form visible chromosomes during cell division

Chapter: Ch2 Cell: The Building Block of Life
Definition: Small organelles present in all active cells; site of protein synthesis; made of RNA and protein; attached to RER or free in cytoplasm

Chapter: Ch2 Cell: The Building Block of Life
Definition: Large network of membrane-bound tubes and sheets in the cytoplasm; transports materials and provides surface for biochemical reactions

Chapter: Ch2 Cell: The Building Block of Life
Definition: ER studded with ribosomes on its surface; site of protein synthesis; synthesised proteins sent to various cell destinations

Chapter: Ch2 Cell: The Building Block of Life
Definition: ER lacking ribosomes; involved in lipid synthesis; plays role in detoxification of poisons in liver cells

Chapter: Ch2 Cell: The Building Block of Life
Definition: Stack of membrane-bound vesicles (cisterns) arranged parallel to each other; modifies, packages and dispatches cell products inside and outside the cell

Chapter: Ch2 Cell: The Building Block of Life
Definition: Membrane-bound sacs filled with digestive enzymes made by RER; break down foreign material and worn-out organelles; called "suicide bags"

Chapter: Ch2 Cell: The Building Block of Life
Definition: Double-membrane organelles that produce ATP through cellular respiration; called "powerhouses of the cell"; have their own DNA and ribosomes

Chapter: Ch2 Cell: The Building Block of Life
Definition: Folds of the inner mitochondrial membrane; increase surface area for ATP-generating chemical reactions

Chapter: Ch2 Cell: The Building Block of Life
Definition: Adenosine triphosphate; energy currency of the cell; stores and releases energy for cellular activities; produced in mitochondria

Chapter: Ch2 Cell: The Building Block of Life
Definition: Double-membrane organelles found only in plant cells; include chloroplasts (for photosynthesis), chromoplasts and leucoplasts; have own DNA

Chapter: Ch2 Cell: The Building Block of Life
Definition: Green plastid containing chlorophyll; site of photosynthesis; internal organisation has stroma with membrane layers

Chapter: Ch2 Cell: The Building Block of Life
Definition: Fluid matrix inside chloroplasts in which membrane layers (thylakoids) are embedded; site of Calvin cycle reactions

Chapter: Ch2 Cell: The Building Block of Life
Definition: Coloured plastids (not green) containing yellow/orange/red pigments; give colour to fruits, flowers and vegetables

Chapter: Ch2 Cell: The Building Block of Life
Definition: Colourless plastids; primarily store starch, oils or protein granules in plant cells

Chapter: Ch2 Cell: The Building Block of Life
Definition: Membrane-bound storage sacs; large in plant cells (occupy 50–90% of volume) storing cell sap; small in animal cells; expel waste in unicellular organisms

Chapter: Ch2 Cell: The Building Block of Life
Definition: Fluid inside plant vacuoles containing sugars, amino acids, organic acids, proteins and waste products; maintains turgidity

Chapter: Ch2 Cell: The Building Block of Life
Definition: Type of cell division producing two genetically identical daughter cells with same chromosome number as parent cell; used for growth and repair

Chapter: Ch2 Cell: The Building Block of Life
Definition: Type of cell division producing four daughter cells each with half the chromosome number of parent; used in gamete formation

Chapter: Ch2 Cell: The Building Block of Life
Definition: Principle stating all living organisms are composed of cells, the cell is the basic unit of life, and all cells arise from pre-existing cells (Schleiden, Schwann, Virchow)

Chapter: Ch2 Cell: The Building Block of Life
Definition: Phenomenon where normal cells stop dividing when they come in contact with neighbouring cells; absent in cancer cells

Chapter: Ch2 Cell: The Building Block of Life
Definition: Ability of a single cell to give rise to a complete organism; basis of plant tissue culture

Chapter: Ch2 Cell: The Building Block of Life
Definition: Reproductive cells (sperm and egg) with half the normal chromosome number; formed by meiosis; fuse during fertilisation

Definition: Diploid cell formed by fusion of male and female gametes; first cell of a new individual
Group of cells similar in structure and/or working together to perform a particular function; e.g., blood, phloem, muscle
Dividing tissue in plants; located at growing tips and certain regions; cells have dense cytoplasm, thin cellulose walls, prominent nuclei and lack vacuoles
Meristematic tissue at tips of roots and shoots; responsible for increasing length of root and stem
Meristematic tissue on the sides of stems/roots (cambium); responsible for increase in girth
Meristematic tissue at nodes; found in some plants like grasses; located near the base of internodes
Process by which meristematic cells become specialised, acquiring permanent shape, size and function; leads to permanent tissue
Plant tissues derived from meristematic tissue after cells lose ability to divide; classified as simple and complex permanent tissue
Plant tissue composed of only one type of cell; includes parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma
Plant tissue composed of more than one cell type working together; includes xylem and phloem; also called vascular tissue
Single outer layer of cells covering all plant organs; protective role; cells form continuous layer without intercellular spaces
Waxy, water-resistant layer secreted by epidermal cells on aerial plant surfaces; aids in protection against water loss, mechanical injury and fungi
Small pores in leaf epidermis through which gaseous exchange (CO₂ and O₂) and transpiration occur; surrounded by guard cells
Kidney-shaped cells flanking each stoma; regulate opening and closing of stomata; necessary for gas exchange and transpiration
Long hair-like extensions of root epidermal cells; greatly increase surface area for absorption of water and minerals
Loss of water vapour from plant surfaces, mainly through stomata; helps in upward movement of water (transpiration pull)
Most common simple permanent tissue; living, thin-walled, loosely arranged cells with intercellular spaces; stores food; site of photosynthesis in leaves
Living permanent tissue with cells irregularly thickened at corners; provides flexibility and mechanical support in plant parts like tendrils and leaf stalks
Dead permanent tissue with heavily lignified cell walls; provides hardness and stiffness to plant parts; e.g., husk of coconut
Complex polymer deposited in cell walls of sclerenchyma and some xylem cells; provides rigidity and waterproofing; walls thicken until no internal space
Complex vascular tissue in plants; transports water and dissolved minerals upward from roots to leaves
Complex vascular tissue in plants; transports food (sugars) made in leaves to all other parts of the plant
Dead xylem cells with lignified walls; long tube-like structures that conduct water; thickened walls with pits
Dead xylem cells joined end-to-end forming long continuous tubes; efficient water-conducting channels in angiosperms
Living xylem cells that store food and assist in lateral conduction of water
Dead xylem cells with thick lignified walls; mainly supportive function in plants
Long tubular phloem cells with perforated walls (sieve plates); principal food-conducting elements; living but lack nucleus at maturity
Living nucleated phloem cells associated with sieve tubes; assist in loading and unloading of food materials into sieve tubes
Living phloem cells that store food and assist in lateral conduction of materials
Dead phloem cells providing mechanical support to phloem tissue; also called bast fibres
Plant tissue system comprising xylem and phloem; forms vascular bundles; responsible for transport of water and food throughout the plant
Animal tissue forming outer covering of body and lining of organs; cells tightly packed with little intercellular space; regulates exchange of materials
Animal tissue with loosely spaced cells embedded in intercellular matrix; connects, supports and transports; e.g., blood, bone, cartilage, ligament
Animal tissue consisting of elongated muscle cells (fibres) capable of contraction and relaxation; responsible for all body movements
Animal tissue composed of neurons; highly specialised for receiving stimuli and transmitting impulses; found in brain, spinal cord and nerves
Voluntary striated muscle attached to bones; multinucleate, cylindrical, unbranched cells with alternate light and dark bands
Involuntary unstriated muscle found in internal organs (gut, blood vessels, iris); spindle-shaped, uninucleate cells
Involuntary, cylindrical, branched, uninucleate muscle found only in the heart; contracts rhythmically throughout life without fatigue
Structural and functional unit of nervous tissue; consists of cell body with nucleus, dendrites (receive impulses) and axon (transmit impulses)
Short, branched extensions of a neuron that receive nerve impulses from other neurons or sense organs
Single long extension of a neuron that transmits nerve impulses away from the cell body toward muscles or other neurons
Hard connective tissue with matrix of calcium and phosphorus compounds; forms skeleton; supports and protects body organs
Flexible connective tissue with protein-sugar matrix; smoothens bone surfaces at joints; present in nose, ear, trachea and larynx
Fibrous connective tissue connecting muscle to bone; strong but has limited flexibility
Elastic connective tissue connecting bone to bone at joints; very elastic with considerable strength
Fluid connective tissue with liquid matrix (plasma) containing RBCs, WBCs and platelets; transports oxygen, food, hormones and waste
Liquid matrix of blood; contains proteins, salts and hormones; approximately 55% of blood volume
Biconcave disc-shaped blood cells containing haemoglobin; transport oxygen from lungs to body cells; lack nucleus when mature
Nucleated blood cells of the immune system; defend body against pathogens and foreign substances; several types (neutrophils, lymphocytes, etc.)
Tiny cell fragments in blood derived from megakaryocytes; help in blood clotting at wound sites to prevent excessive blood loss
Iron-containing protein in red blood cells; binds oxygen in lungs and releases it to tissues; gives blood its red colour
Concentric rings visible in cross-section of tree stems; each ring represents one year's growth by lateral meristem; used to determine tree age
Secondary meristem in the cortex of older stems; produces cork cells that replace epidermis as outer protective layer
Dead, compactly arranged cells produced by cork cambium; have suberin in walls making them impermeable to gases and water
Point on a plant stem where one or more leaves are attached; also site of intercalary meristem in some plants
Region of stem between two successive nodes; no leaf attachment; contains mainly permanent tissue
Biological process by which organisms produce new individuals of their own kind; fundamental characteristic of life; ensures continuation of species
Asexual reproduction in plants where new plants develop from vegetative parts (roots, stems, leaves); produces genetically identical offspring
Method of vegetative propagation where a piece of stem or leaf is planted to develop roots and grow into a new plant
Vegetative propagation joining shoot (scion) of one plant to rooted stem (stock) of another; combines desired traits from two plants
Vegetative propagation where a stem is bent to soil and allowed to develop roots before being separated from parent plant
Technique of growing plant cells or tissues in sterile artificial nutrient medium outside the organism; produces clones; basis of totipotency
Asexual reproduction where a new organism develops as an outgrowth (bud) from the parent and separates; e.g., Hydra, yeast
Asexual reproduction producing small, light, resistant spores (in sporangia) that develop into new organisms under favourable conditions
Reproduction involving a single parent without formation of gametes; offspring are genetically identical clones of the parent
Reproduction involving fusion of male and female gametes from two parents; introduces genetic variation in offspring
Flowering plants with seeds enclosed inside a fruit; most diverse and advanced plant group; flowers are reproductive structures
Leaf-like outermost whorl of a flower (calyx); usually green; protects the flower bud before it opens
Often coloured part of a flower (corolla); attracts pollinators (insects, birds) for pollination
Male reproductive organ of a flower; consists of anther (produces pollen) and filament (stalk)
Pollen-producing part at the top of the stamen; contains pollen sacs where pollen grains (male gametes) develop
Female reproductive organ of a flower; consists of stigma, style and ovary; also called carpel
Sticky top part of pistil; receives pollen grains during pollination; begins pollen tube growth
Stalk-like part of pistil connecting stigma to ovary; pollen tube grows through it to reach the ovule
Bottom swollen part of pistil containing ovules; develops into fruit after fertilisation
Structure inside the ovary containing the egg cell; develops into seed after fertilisation by male gamete
Transfer of pollen grains from anther to stigma of a flower; prerequisite for fertilisation in angiosperms
Transfer of pollen from anther to stigma of the same flower or another flower on the same plant
Transfer of pollen from anther of one plant to stigma of a different plant of the same species; increases genetic variation
Agents (wind, insects, birds, water) that carry pollen from anther to stigma enabling pollination
Tube formed by germinating pollen grain on the stigma; grows down through style to the ovule for fertilisation
Fusion of male gamete (from pollen) with female gamete (egg cell in ovule) to form a diploid zygote
Diploid cell formed by fusion of male and female gametes; divides mitotically to form embryo
Early stage of multicellular organism development from the zygote; enclosed within the seed; develops into a new plant on germination
Mature ripened ovary containing seeds; develops after fertilisation; aids in protection and dispersal of seeds
Mature ovule containing the embryo and stored food (endosperm); protected by seed coat (testa); unit of dispersal and reproduction
Process by which a seed develops into a seedling under favourable conditions of water, warmth and light
Scattering of seeds away from parent plant by wind, water, animals or explosive mechanisms; prevents overcrowding and competition
Fertilisation occurring outside the body in an aquatic medium; e.g., in frogs, fish; requires water for gamete transfer
Fertilisation occurring inside the female body; e.g., in birds, reptiles and mammals including humans
Primary male reproductive organs that produce sperm and secrete testosterone; located in the scrotum
External sac below the abdomen housing the testes; maintains temperature ~2–3°C lower than body temperature for sperm production
Tube (ductus deferens) that carries sperm from testes to urethra during ejaculation
Male gamete produced in testes; has head (DNA), middle piece (mitochondria) and tail (flagellum) for motility
Primary female reproductive organs that produce eggs (ova) and hormones (oestrogen, progesterone)
Fallopian tubes; carry eggs released from ovaries to uterus; site of fertilisation in humans
Muscular pear-shaped organ where fertilised egg implants and the embryo/foetus develops during pregnancy
Release of a mature egg from the ovary; occurs approximately on day 14 of a 28-day menstrual cycle
Approximately 28-day cycle of changes in the female reproductive system including ovulation, preparation of uterine lining and menstruation
Monthly shedding of the uterine lining (endometrium) when fertilisation does not occur; lasts approximately 3–5 days
Embedding of the fertilised egg (blastocyst) into the thickened uterine wall; marks beginning of pregnancy
Temporary organ connecting foetus to mother's uterine wall; exchanges nutrients, oxygen and waste between mother and foetus
Methods used to prevent pregnancy; includes barrier (condom), hormonal (pills) and intrauterine (IUD/Copper-T) devices
Sexually transmitted infections spread through sexual contact; e.g., HIV/AIDS, gonorrhoea, syphilis; condom provides protection
XX (female) and XY (male) chromosomes that determine biological sex; the Y chromosome from the father determines male offspring
Variety of life on Earth at genetic, species and ecosystem levels; approximately 1.7–1.8 million known and described species
Species found naturally only in a particular region or habitat and nowhere else in the world
Regions with exceptionally high levels of species richness, high endemism and significant habitat loss
Systematic arrangement of living organisms into groups based on shared characteristics and evolutionary relationships
System proposed by Whittaker (1969) dividing organisms into Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia based on cell structure and nutrition
Kingdom of prokaryotic organisms (bacteria and cyanobacteria); lack membrane-bound nucleus; earliest evolved group
Kingdom of mostly single-celled eukaryotes; e.g., Amoeba, Paramecium, Spirogyra, diatoms; includes algae and protozoans
Kingdom of non-photosynthetic eukaryotes with chitin cell walls; decomposers; body made of mycelium/hyphae; e.g., mushrooms, Rhizopus
Kingdom of multicellular, autotrophic eukaryotes with cellulose cell walls; photosynthesis using chlorophyll; includes all plants
Kingdom of multicellular, heterotrophic eukaryotes without cell walls; ingest food; includes all animals
Prokaryotic single-celled organisms in Kingdom Monera; diverse shapes (cocci, bacilli, spirilla, vibrio); found everywhere
Photosynthetic prokaryotes (blue-green algae) in Kingdom Monera; can fix atmospheric nitrogen; e.g., Nostoc, Anabaena
Algae; most primitive plant division with no differentiation into root, stem and leaf; e.g., Spirogyra, Chara, Ulva
Mosses and liverworts; simple land plants with no vascular tissue; called amphibians of the plant kingdom; e.g., Funaria, Marchantia
Ferns and horsetails; first vascular plants; reproduce by spores; no seeds; e.g., Dryopteris, Equisetum
Vascular plants producing naked seeds not enclosed in a fruit; e.g., Pinus, Cycas; seeds in cones
Flowering plants with seeds enclosed inside fruits; divided into monocots and dicots; most dominant plant group
Sponges; simplest multicellular animals with pores throughout the body; no true tissues; e.g., Sycon, Spongilla
Radially symmetrical animals with stinging cells (cnidoblasts); two cell layers; e.g., Hydra, jellyfish, sea anemone, corals
Flatworms; bilaterally symmetrical, dorsoventrally flattened, triploblastic, acoelomate; e.g., tapeworm, Planaria, liver fluke
Roundworms; cylindrical, unsegmented body, pseudocoelomate; e.g., Ascaris, Wuchereria (filarial worm)
Segmented worms with true coelom and metamerism; e.g., earthworm (Lumbricus), leech (Hirudinaria)
Largest animal phylum; jointed appendages, exoskeleton of chitin; e.g., insects, crustaceans, spiders, centipedes
Soft-bodied, usually shelled animals; e.g., Pila (apple snail), Unio, Octopus, Sepia
Spiny-skinned marine animals; water vascular system; pentaradial symmetry; e.g., starfish, sea urchin, sea cucumber
Animals with notochord but no true vertebral column; e.g., Amphioxus (Branchiostoma), Balanoglossus
Animals with a vertebral column (backbone) derived from notochord; includes fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals
Flexible rod-like supportive structure present at some stage in all chordates; replaced by vertebral column in vertebrates
Complex polysaccharide forming cell walls of fungi and the exoskeleton of arthropods
Network of thread-like hyphae forming the vegetative body of a fungus
Thread-like filaments forming the mycelium of fungi; responsible for absorption of nutrients
Organisms that obtain nutrition by secreting enzymes onto dead and decaying organic matter and absorbing the products
System of giving each organism a two-part Latin scientific name: genus (capitalised) + species (lowercase); proposed by Carolus Linnaeus
18th-century Swedish botanist who developed modern taxonomy and binomial nomenclature; "Father of Taxonomy"
Taxonomic rank above species and below family; groups closely related species; e.g., Homo (humans and fossil relatives)
Basic unit of biological classification; group of organisms capable of interbreeding and producing fertile offspring
Preserved remains or traces of past organisms found in sedimentary rocks; evidence for evolutionary history
Symbiotic association between a fungus and a photosynthetic alga or cyanobacterium; indicator species for air quality
Seven levels of classification from broadest to most specific: Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species
Integrated system of four interconnected spheres: geosphere, hydrosphere, cryosphere and atmosphere, which interact to support life
Solid part of Earth including rocks, minerals, soil and Earth's interior; source of nutrients for living organisms
All water on Earth including oceans, rivers, lakes, groundwater, ice and water vapour; covers ~71% of Earth's surface
Frozen water component of the Earth system: ice caps, glaciers, sea ice, permafrost and snowpack
Layer of gases surrounding Earth held by gravity; mainly nitrogen (78%) and oxygen (21%); regulates temperature and shields UV
Zone of life on Earth; thin layer at the intersection of other spheres where living organisms exist and interact
Incoming solar radiation received at Earth's surface; primary energy source driving weather, climate and photosynthesis
Fraction of incoming solar radiation reflected by a surface; ice/snow have high albedo; dark surfaces have low albedo
Gases (CO₂, CH₄, N₂O, water vapour) that absorb and re-radiate infrared radiation; trap heat in atmosphere
Natural warming of Earth's surface when greenhouse gases in atmosphere trap outgoing infrared radiation; essential for life
Rise in Earth's average surface temperature due to enhanced greenhouse effect from burning fossil fuels and deforestation
Region in stratosphere (15–35 km altitude) containing O₃; absorbs most harmful UV radiation protecting life on Earth
Region of severely depleted ozone concentration over Antarctica; caused mainly by CFCs reacting with ozone
Chlorofluorocarbons; synthetic industrial chemicals used in refrigerants and aerosols; break down stratospheric ozone when released
1987 international treaty to phase out ozone-depleting substances; considered highly successful in reducing CFC emissions
Cyclic movement of chemical elements (C, N, O, water) between biotic (living) and abiotic (non-living) components of ecosystems
Continuous movement of water through evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation and runoff between ocean, atmosphere and land
Circulation of carbon through atmosphere (CO₂), biosphere (photosynthesis/respiration), oceans and geosphere (fossil fuels/carbonates)
Movement of nitrogen through atmosphere (N₂), soil and living organisms via fixation, nitrification, assimilation and denitrification
Conversion of atmospheric N₂ into biologically usable ammonia (NH₃) or nitrates by bacteria (Rhizobium, Azotobacter) or lightning
Conversion of ammonia to nitrites by Nitrosomonas and then to nitrates by Nitrobacter; makes nitrogen available to plants
Conversion of nitrates in soil back to atmospheric N₂ gas by bacteria such as Pseudomonas; returns nitrogen to atmosphere
Decomposition of dead organic nitrogen-containing compounds to ammonia by decomposers; first step in returning nitrogen to soil
Nitrogen-fixing bacteria living in symbiotic relationship in root nodules of leguminous plants (peas, beans, clover)
Free-living nitrogen-fixing bacteria in soil; convert atmospheric N₂ to ammonia without a host plant
Nitrifying bacteria that oxidise ammonia (NH₃) to nitrites (NO₂⁻) in the nitrogen cycle
Nitrifying bacteria that oxidise nitrites (NO₂⁻) to nitrates (NO₃⁻) available for plant uptake
Denitrifying bacteria that convert nitrates back to atmospheric N₂; complete the nitrogen cycle
Excessive growth of algae (algal bloom) and depletion of dissolved oxygen in water bodies due to enrichment with N and P from agricultural runoff
Large-scale removal of forests; increases atmospheric CO₂, reduces biodiversity, causes soil erosion and disrupts water cycle
Coal, oil and natural gas; formed from ancient organic matter over millions of years; release CO₂ when burned; non-renewable
Phenomenon where urban areas are significantly warmer than surrounding rural areas due to heat-absorbing surfaces and human activities
Lowest atmospheric layer (0–12 km); where weather occurs; temperature decreases with altitude; contains most atmospheric mass
Atmospheric layer above troposphere (12–50 km); contains ozone layer; temperature increases with altitude; little weather
Graph showing continuous rise in atmospheric CO₂ concentration since 1958; measured by Charles Keeling at Mauna Loa, Hawaii

Definition: Organisms whose cells have a true nucleus with nuclear membrane and membrane-bound organelles; e.g., all plants, animals, fungi, protists

Definition: Fluid content inside the plasma membrane; contains organelles; site of many metabolic reactions

Group of cells similar in structure and/or function; arranged to give highest efficiency for that function; e.g., blood, muscle, xylem
Plant tissue that continuously divides; located at growing regions; cells have dense cytoplasm, thin walls, no vacuoles
Growing tips of roots and shoots; cells divide to increase length; most active meristem
Cambium; adds to girth of stem and root by producing secondary xylem and phloem
Meristematic tissue at nodes, near base of internodes; found in some monocots like grasses
Process of taking up a permanent shape, size and function; transforms meristematic cells into permanent tissue cells
Tissue whose cells have lost the ability to divide; derived from meristematic tissue through differentiation
Simple permanent tissue; living, thin-walled cells with intercellular spaces; stores food; most abundant plant tissue
Parenchyma containing chloroplasts; performs photosynthesis; found in leaves and outer layers of young stems
Parenchyma in aquatic plants with large air cavities; helps plants float and enables gas exchange underwater
Living permanent tissue; cells with irregular thickening at corners; provides flexibility and mechanical support without being brittle
Dead permanent tissue; cells with uniformly thick lignified walls; makes plant parts hard and stiff; e.g., coconut husk
Hard, waterproof polymer deposited in secondary cell walls; responsible for woodiness and stiffness in sclerenchyma and xylem
Outer single-layer covering of plant body; protective; cells compact without intercellular spaces; secretes cuticle
Waxy water-resistant layer on outer surface of epidermal cells; reduces water loss; absent in underwater plants
Pores in leaf epidermis; surrounded by guard cells; allow gaseous exchange and transpiration
Kidney-shaped cells bordering stomata; control opening/closing of stoma; only epidermal cells with chloroplasts
Chemical substance with waterproof quality coating epidermis of desert plants; reduces water loss in dry habitats
Dead protective tissue in older plant stems; produced by cork cambium; has suberin-impregnated walls; replaces epidermis
Fatty substance in cork cell walls; makes them impervious to water and gases; responsible for cork's protective properties
Complex plant tissue transporting water and minerals upward; consists of tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma and xylem fibres
Complex plant tissue transporting food (sugars) from leaves; consists of sieve tubes, companion cells, phloem parenchyma and phloem fibres
Long dead xylem cells with pitted lignified walls; conduct water; present in all vascular plants
Tubular dead xylem cells joined end-to-end; efficient water conductors in angiosperms; wider than tracheids
Tubular phloem cells with perforated sieve plates; food-conducting; living but enucleate (lack nucleus) at maturity
Nucleated living cells alongside sieve tubes; assist in loading and unloading food into/out of sieve tubes
Covering tissue in animals; forms lining of body surfaces and organs; cells tightly packed; regulates material exchange
Flat thin epithelial cells; lines blood vessels, lung alveoli and cheek (simple squamous); skin (stratified squamous)
Tall pillar-like epithelial cells lining intestine; facilitates absorption; may bear cilia (ciliated columnar) in respiratory tract
Cube-shaped epithelial cells lining kidney tubules and salivary gland ducts; provides mechanical support
Epithelial cells specialised for secretion; fold inward to form multicellular glands; e.g., sweat glands, salivary glands
Animal tissue with cells in a matrix (fluid, dense or rigid); connects and supports other tissues; e.g., blood, bone, cartilage
Fluid connective tissue; plasma matrix with RBCs, WBCs and platelets; transports gases, nutrients, hormones and waste
Fluid matrix of blood; contains dissolved proteins, salts and hormones; suspends blood cells
RBCs; biconcave cells with haemoglobin; transport oxygen; lack nucleus in mammals
WBCs; nucleated immune cells in blood; several types (neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, etc.); defend against infection
Cell fragments in blood; involved in blood clotting; released from megakaryocytes in bone marrow
Rigid connective tissue; matrix of calcium and phosphorus compounds; bone cells (osteocytes) in Haversian canals; forms skeleton
Flexible connective tissue; matrix of proteins and sugars; chondrocytes embedded in it; at joints, nose, ear, trachea
Elastic connective tissue connecting bone to bone; contains little matrix; very strong
Fibrous connective tissue connecting muscle to bone; strong with limited flexibility
Loose connective tissue filling spaces between skin and muscles, around blood vessels/nerves; supports internal organs; aids repair
Fat-storing connective tissue below skin and between organs; acts as energy reserve and thermal insulator
Voluntary, striated muscle attached to bones; cylindrical, multinucleate, unbranched cells; moves limbs and body parts
Involuntary, unstriated muscle in internal organs (digestive tract, blood vessels, iris); spindle-shaped, uninucleate
Involuntary, branched, cylindrical, uninucleate muscle of heart; shows rhythmic contraction throughout life
Structural unit of nervous tissue; cell body with nucleus and cytoplasm, one axon and many dendrites; up to 1 metre long
Short branched processes of neuron receiving impulses from other neurons; multiple per neuron
Single long process of neuron transmitting impulse away from cell body toward other neurons or effectors
Electrical signal travelling along a neuron; allows rapid communication between different body parts; enables coordinated responses
Crossing between genetically dissimilar plants to combine desirable characteristics; may be intervarietal, interspecific or intergeneric
Crossing between different varieties of the same crop species; common method of crop improvement
Crossing between two different species of the same genus; produces new combinations of traits
Crossing between plants belonging to different genera; produces distant hybrids
Crops developed by introducing a specific gene from another organism to provide a desired characteristic (e.g., pest resistance)
Crops grown during rainy season from June to October; e.g., paddy, soyabean, maize, cotton, green gram, black gram
Crops grown during winter season from November to April; e.g., wheat, gram, peas, mustard, linseed
Plant nutrients required in large quantities; include nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium, sulphur; supplied by soil
Plant nutrients required in small quantities; include iron, manganese, boron, zinc, copper, molybdenum, chlorine
Organic material prepared by decomposition of animal excreta and plant waste; improves soil structure and adds nutrients
Decomposed organic farm waste (livestock excreta, vegetable waste, domestic waste) rich in organic matter; used as soil enricher
Compost prepared with earthworms to hasten decomposition of plant and animal refuse; nutrient-rich organic fertiliser
Plants (e.g., sun hemp, guar) grown and ploughed back into soil before sowing main crop; enriches soil with nitrogen and phosphorus
Commercially produced chemicals supplying nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium; ensure vegetative growth; can cause water pollution if overused
Farming system using minimal or no synthetic chemicals; relies on organic manures, bio-agents, and mixed/intercropping systems
Growing two or more crops simultaneously on the same field; e.g., wheat + gram; reduces risk of total crop failure
Growing two or more crops in definite row patterns on the same field; crops have different nutrient requirements; prevents pest/disease spread
Growing different crops on the same land in a planned sequence over successive seasons; maintains soil fertility and controls pests
Unwanted plants in cultivated fields that compete with crops for nutrients, space, water and light; reduce crop yield
Chemicals used to control agricultural pests; includes herbicides (weeds), insecticides (insects) and fungicides (fungi)
Scientific management of animal livestock including proper feeding, breeding, disease control and housing for increased production
Female dairy animals used for milk production; e.g., cows (Bos indicus) and buffaloes (Bos bubalis)
Animals used for farm labour such as tilling, irrigation and carting; e.g., bullocks, horses
Period of milk production after birth of a young one; longer lactation in exotic breeds like Jersey, Brown Swiss
Raising domestic fowl (chickens, ducks) for egg production (layers) and meat production (broilers)
Poultry birds raised for meat; fed protein-rich, vitamin A and K supplemented diet; fast growth rate
Poultry birds raised for egg production; different management requirements from broilers
Obtaining fish from natural marine or freshwater resources using fishing nets; guided by satellites and echo-sounders
Controlled cultivation of fish through aquaculture in ponds, tanks, lagoons or marine environments
Culture of marine organisms (fish, shellfish, seaweed) in seawater; e.g., prawns, mussels, oysters, mullets
System using 5–6 fish species with different feeding habits in one pond; Catla (surface), Rohu (middle), Mrigal and Common Carp (bottom) and Grass Carp (weeds)
Maintaining bee colonies (apiaries) to obtain honey and wax; low-investment additional income for farmers
Flowers available to bees for collecting nectar and pollen; quality and taste of honey depends on the type of pasturage
Farm or site where beehives are maintained for commercial honey production
Availability of and access to sufficient nutritious food for all people; requires both adequate production and equitable distribution
Dramatic increase in food-grain production in India from 1950s–70s through high-yielding varieties, fertilizers and irrigation
